tour.title: Guided tours
tour.inviteBody: New here? A two-minute tour shows you how the app is laid out.

welcome.title: Two minutes, then you are on your own
welcome.body: This points at the real screen, so anything you see here is where it will be tomorrow. Escape closes the tour at any moment; the arrow keys move between steps.

nav.title: Three groups, not one long list
nav.body: Top: what you own. Middle: what happens to it — asking, buying, forecasting, using. Bottom: settings and the record of everything. You only ever see what your role allows.

metrics.title: The state of things, in four numbers
metrics.body: Active concepts, items, open containers, and how many things are running low. If the last one is red, something is at zero.

tree.title: The tree is a filter
tree.body: Click a room and every number on this page narrows to that room and everything under it. Click it again to let go.

cards.title: One card per concept
cards.body: Not per item — per thing you need. Anything low or empty opens itself, because the alert is the reason to look. Expand a card to open or empty an individual container.

quickAdd.title: Adding things is one box
quickAdd.body: Type what arrived. If it exists, it is found; if it does not, the app creates the whole chain behind it. It stays open for the next one, and the q key opens it from anywhere.

fastKey.title: Signing in without typing
fastKey.body: Give yourself a key chord here and two clusters of keys sign you in — press the same chord again and it signs you out. It is how a shared bench changes hands in a second. Treat it like a door code: it is a shortcut, not a password.

help.title: The manual lives here
help.body: Behind this button: the full written manual in your language, and these tours. They are marked off as you finish them.

remember.title: Your own desk, or a shared one
remember.body: A computer nobody has claimed signs you out after twenty minutes of silence, so the next person’s work is not filed under your name. Claim this one with your password and it stays signed in as you through shutdowns and reboots. Only you, and only here.

look.title: The look of the place
look.body: Admins drop your logo in here and the app reads three colour schemes straight out of it — one click and every computer in the building wears them. Under that, your own three colours, kept in this browser only.

intro.title: Every physical thing you own
intro.body: One row per container, per instrument, per document. The id on the left is the app’s own — it is what a label sticks to and what History remembers.

filters.title: Filter, then act
filters.body: Type, concept, variant, place, status, free text. Every dropdown takes typing, accents and all, so finding one glue among two hundred things is four letters rather than a scroll. Filters combine: “open tins in the flammables cupboard” is four clicks and no query language.

drawer.title: Clicking a row opens everything
drawer.body: Its whole record, the fields its Type defines, its own history — and the buttons that change it. Nothing about an item is edited anywhere else.

statuses.title: Open, then empty
statuses.body: Those two buttons are the whole daily routine. Status is never typed by hand: each one is an action the app records, with who and when.

request.title: Emptying the last one asks for more
request.body: The moment you know you need something is the moment the bottle runs out — so that is when the request form appears, already filled in. You never go looking for it.

sorting.title: Any column, either way
sorting.body: Click a heading to sort by it, click again to reverse, a third time to let go. It sorts every matching item, not the page you are looking at — so “the oldest bottle we still have” is one click, wherever it happens to be.

requests.title: A request is “we need wood glue”
requests.body: Nothing about brands or prices: it is made against the concept, so the person who needs it does not have to know what to buy. If somebody already asked, you add yourself to theirs instead of writing a second one.

lots.title: A lot is one order to one shop
lots.body: Tick the requests it covers and they become lines. Requests name a concept, an order names a product — so this is where you say which brand and which size, picking what you bought last time or naming a new one on the spot. It is remembered for next time either way.

receive.title: Receiving is where it pays off
receive.body: Say how many of each line arrived and the app creates the items: ids, prices, location, expiry. Twelve bottles without typing twelve items. Short deliveries and substitutions are expected, not errors.

forecast.title: What runs out before you can reorder it
forecast.body: Measured from real depletions, with the supplier’s own average delivery time. No chart: a list, and one button that turns the whole list into requests.

loop.title: And that closes the circle
loop.body: Request → lot → items → they run out → the forecast notices → request. Nobody has to remember to start it; the empty bottle does.

intro.title: Not everything is stock
intro.body: A caliper is an item too, but “0 calipers in stock” was never a warning worth showing. Tools and documents stay off this screen — except for one thing.

due.title: Except when something is due
due.body: Overdue maintenance sits above your stock, because a machine out of calibration stops work in a way a low bottle does not. When nothing is due, the band is not there at all.

tab.title: The Equipment tab
tab.body: Every item has one. It holds what belongs with this thing — its manual, its spares, its accessories — and what has to be done to it on a schedule.

plans.title: Every N days, or every N uses
plans.body: Or both, and then it falls due whichever runs out first — which is what “every 6 months or 500 holes” actually means. Marking it done restarts both counters and writes a line into the service history.

places.title: And where everything is
places.body: The tree describes your workshop; picking a node shows what is in it, with or without the shelves underneath. This answers the question you have standing in front of a cupboard.

fastKey.title: Fast login key
fastKey.intro: Two clusters of keys, held down one after the other, sign you in without typing anything. Press them again while signed in and they sign you out — so handing the machine to the next person is one gesture each.
fastKey.none: You have no key chord yet.
fastKey.howToPress: Hold the first cluster together, let go, then hold the second. Chords are chosen by the app so that no two people share one, and so that each cluster fits under one hand.
fastKey.practiceHint: Try it here — nothing happens either way.
fastKey.practiceMiss: Not quite. Hold all the keys down together until they register.
fastKey.holdNote: Stored on this computer, not on your account — it belongs to this keyboard.
fastKey.warning: Treat it like the key to the workshop door: anyone who watches you press it can sign in as you. It is a shortcut, not a password — your password still works, and an admin can revoke a chord at any time.
fastKey.loginHint: If you have a fast login key, press it now — no need to click anything first.
fastKey.unknown: That key chord belongs to nobody
fastKey.throttled: Too many attempts. Wait a minute, or sign in with your password.
fastKey.failed: Fast login failed. Sign in with your password.
fastKey.revokeHint: Remove this person’s fast login key
